Don't let your past haunt you...

I made a stupid- inexcusably stupid- mistake at work. No. "Mistake" isn't right, because that implies some kind of accident or oversight. There are some factors involved- it was my first professional job and the office environment was unprofessional to the point of toxic, so there was literally no opportunity for me to learn good professional behavior there. But those are factors, not excuses. What I did was stupid. And it got me fired. Justifiably. The guy was looking for an excuse to fire everyone in our department- he wanted to replace us with friends of his on contract at huge rates. But I made it easy for him- and justifiable.

We lived in a city with a pretty crappy economy and there were no decent jobs to be had. In fact, two or three major local employers had just closed up shop, so there was a lot of competition for crappy jobs. I was turned down for unemployment. We were so poor that my wife and I literally ate on alternating days so that our daughter could eat every day. ADC, WIC, etc having also all declined to help. I finally gave up and moved to another city to crash on a friend's couch while I looked for a real job in a city that had them. In the meantime, I delivered pizzas because I could usually count on something being left over at the end of the night. Which meant I got to eat. I saw my wife and daughter on weekends only. They hadn't moved yet because my wife still had a job, albeit a crappy one, and we still had our house. We only saw each other on weekends. I don't know which was worse. Me getting home and seeing how happy my daughter was because she didn't see much of me, or getting home and not getting much of a reaction because she was used to me not being around. I found a job in my field only to watch the company go under within six months. During that time, my wife was laid off. Because of that, we lost the house, but at least we were living together again.

I got things on track again by trial and error. I learned what worked in interviews and with recruiters, and what did not. I spent a fair amount of our dwindling cash reserves on a better suit so I could look decent when walking into an interview. I practiced explaining my recent unemployment situation in the best way possible without lying. In the meantime, I went back to pizzas since working a shit job is far better than starving. And I networked. Met everyone I could who I thought could help in any way. Finally started meeting people who were willing to give me an interview, and finally got one of them right and got the job. Al in all, the "bad times" as we call them now, lasted about a year and a half, but the consequences lasted far longer. Things are fine now- hell, considering what we went through then, things are pretty damn awesome now. But there's no two ways about the fact that all this happened because I epically fucked up!

Okay, first off working in a toxic environment can do so much damage to your psyche, I get that. You've gone through so much, and what you said about a year and a half of hardship staying with you for the rest of your life, that has kind of shaken me up. I can't begin to put myself in your shoes.

Staying away from home and your child, you're really strong to do that. Or maybe it's the whole when you have to grit your teeth and just do it. Networking works wonders doesn't it? I'm glad things are fine. Have you forgiven yourself for your mistake? I think you should, even though I'm just a random person on the internet, what you went through is more than what you deserved.

Yes- that environment was damaging. Fact of the matter is, though, I knew I was doing something wrong. Don't get me wrong, though- this hasn't stayed with me the rest of my life. We had our house foreclosed. We paid the price for that for the next 7 years because we knew we wouldn't be able to get a mortgage until that was gone. As a result, we bought our next- current, in fact- house much later in life than average and we've had to do some extraordinary planning to make sure that I'm not still paying for this house when I'm in my seventies.

A lot of good has come from it, though. My wife and I like to say that we don't have to believe that we can survive anything because we've already survived so much. Whatever may come next, divorce won't be a part of it. And while my daughter only knows about this time as something she's been told and vaguely remembers, I remember it well enough to understand that it's better to be a dad in a shitty situation than it is to not be one at all.

My career is solid now. I've been doing what I do for almost 16 years, am somewhat known- not any kind of rock star, but I occasionally have "Hey- I know you" moments at professional conferences. Mainly because I've learned that you're of no use to anyone if you can't be trusted and if you can't work well with others. Dr. House is a fantasy- no one is good enough to be an unreliable loner.

We've also done a lot to future-proof our life. We do well now, but we live simply. It's not that we don't enjoy having things, it's just that we learned early on that disaster can strike out of nowhere. As a result, we're not frivolous. Our house isn't large, and it's certainly not expensive. We have one used car which is of good quality and paid off. We have another that we bought new, but it's a modest sedan that's more reliable than flashy. And it could all come tumbling down tomorrow, and we will be fine. My wife makes enough to keep the house, we could get rid of the car we're still paying on, and we'd have a place to live and money to buy groceries and pay the utilities.

But forgive myself? I know I should, but I'm not wired that way. I've made three major, life-altering, mistakes in life. Not the small, or even moderate, crap that you really wish you hadn't done, but three that had serious consequences for decades. Literally. I'm keenly aware of the fact that getting a second chance in life is one thing, but getting a third is something you take seriously.

<h3>Blogs</h3>

App store optimization: climbing the app store rankings with organic marketing

Dave Bell of Gummicube, doesn't believe in paid app installation campaigns. Find out how he uses App Store optimization to obtain organic users. The reason he trusts this method is because he thinks organically acquired users are better to monetize. This guide will tell you how to apply his techniques to your own app or game.

4 Soft Launch Metrics That Matter to the Success of Your Mobile Game

Soft launching your game is a tried and tested technique. Pepe Agell evangilises soft launching your mobile game and tells you how to do it best. You need to watch your early retention rates and measure your other key metrics. Pepe tells you all this and more!

Marketing 101 for Indie Mobile Game Developers

If you're about to launch your game, you definitely need to check out this article by Rodolfo E. Madero. All your bases are covered with this post, from game reviews to ad campaigns, find out how to market your game on every available channel. This really is a 101 course on marketing your game.

Making pirates feel bad using Android push notifications

The Battlestar: Harbinger team had a problem with piracy. Despite being featured in the iOS App Store and the Google Play Store in their first week of release, they soon had more pirate users than paying users. Find out how they used push notifications to fight this.

Targeting Your Way to Successful App User Acquisition

How well do you know your users? Maggie Mesa tells us about targeted user acquisiiton and why it's important to know your users. She also details how to plan for long-term engagement and measuring results. Find out how to multiply your data.

Pulled taut: the monetisation of Angry Birds 2

In this IAP Inspector, Matt Suckley takes a look at Angry Birds 2. He examines the effects of changing from a premium game to a Free-to-Play model. He takes a very close look at incentives or pressure applied to make in-app purchases, their perceived value, the expansion offered by IAPs and the overall value of the experience.

<h3>News</h3>

Amazon Underground offers new business model for apps and games based on pay per usage

Amazon Underground was launched for Android this week with a new business model. The in-app items, which users usually have to purchase, are now available for free in the games and apps available in Underground. Pay per play usage will be used by Amazon to compensate developers.

Google Launches YouTube Gaming on iOS, Android, Web

After announcing Youtube Gaming in June 2015, the platform has now come to mobile devices. It looks to take on Twitch as a way to stream mobile gaming. Each game has its own page or hub within the app, giving users access to the game’s description, current live streams and popular related videos. Users can also access 'let’s plays', video reviews and more.

FBI: Disgruntled former Game of War manager arrested, accused of stealing trade secrets

The FBI arrested a former manager of <em>Game of War: Fire Age,</em> developer Machine Zone on Aug. 20, alleging that Jing Zeng stole trade secrets after finding out his position would be terminated. This is according to documents unsealed this week and uncovered by The Wall Street Journal.
